newsitem.title: USA: Stocks set to ring in summer.
newsitem.headline: Stocks set to ring in summer.

text.p: Wall Street appears set to ring in the official start of summer this week with yet more gains, as investors refuse to be anything but unswervingly upbeat about prospects for the nation's economy.
As summer begins and the second quarter comes to a close, analysts said recently robust stock prices could push deeper into record territory simply because they lack good reasons to go down.

"It is hard to get this market thrown off the upward trend it is on," Douglas Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at J.P. Morgan said. "It has had a very positive tone ... I think there will be another upward tilt next week."

Stocks might trip if a big company warned of lower earnings or if it seems likely the Federal Reserve will interest rates at its July 1-2 meeting. But otherwise, analysts said, investors will continue to buy.
The Dow industrials closed up 19.45 points at a record 7,796.51 on Friday, bouncing back in the last two days of the week from three down sessions. The blue-chip gauge ended the week up 14.47 points.
Stock prices have rallied as a growing number of investors believe the economy is showing a magic combination of steady growth and tame inflation, analysts said.

"The fundamentals that have been helping the market move higher are pretty sound, and most investors are becoming increasingly convinced of it," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.
Given the economic picture, analysts said there was a growing consensus the Fed would not raise interest rates. This was supporting shares and bonds, they said.
A healthy flow of funds into mutual funds have also kept stocks moving higher, they said.

"Money keeps pouring into mutual funds in general and into index funds in particular," Johnson said. "Because index funds need to stay fully-invested, there is a lot of ammunition to keep this momentum going next week."
J.P. Morgan's Cliggott agreed, saying: "There is a mismatch between buyers and sellers. People are resistant to sell and buyer demand has created upward pressure on prices."
But the positive scenario was not without its downside risks, analysts said.
If durable goods data for May, due out on Wednesday, were very strong, stocks and bonds could fall on worries about uncontrolled and inflationary economic growth, analysts said.
In April, durable goods rose 1.3 percent.
A.C. Moore, chief investment strategist at Principal Financial Securities, said stocks were also starting to look tired after all their recent gains.

"We could see a down draft at the start of the week, then an improvement towards the end of the week, as money managers start to buy their favourite blue-chip names," he said. "But stocks are very extended here."
While Moore said stocks normally performed well near the end of the quarter, a profit warnings, particularly from the technology sector, could hurt the market.
Last week, technology firms Seagate Technology Inc. and Gateway 2000 Inc. spooked the sector when they said their quarterly results would fall short of expectations.
